title: The Stative in Sentences
short: The stative usually follows a noun or pronoun subject, often after jw or mk: mk wj jj.kj "look, I have come".
trouble: Students look for the subject after the stative. The subject comes first; the stative follows like an adjective.

blocks.html: The stative has its endings (Stative Endings) and its meaning (What the Stative Means). Now, where does it stand in a sentence?

The stative follows its subject, like an adjective after a noun. The subject is a noun or a pronoun, often after jw or mk: mk wj jj.kj "look, I have come"; jw=f jj.w "he has come"; jw zꜣt=j ꜥḥꜥ.tj "my daughter is standing".

The stative describes its subject the way an adjective does, so it goes where a description goes, after the thing described. This is the same order as in the adverbial sentence, z m pr "the man is in the house": subject first, then what is said about it. Gardiner groups subject + stative with subject + ḥr + infinitive as one family, the pseudo-verbal construction (The Pseudoverbal Construction).

blocks.cap: mk wj "look, I…": mk takes a dependent pronoun, which can be the subject of a stative.

blocks.title: Find the subject
blocks.q: In mk sw ꜥnḫ.w "look, he is alive", what is the subject of ꜥnḫ.w?
steps: The subject comes before the stative.
After mk it is a dependent pronoun: sw "him, he".

blocks.title: Write it
blocks.q: Write "My daughter is standing" with jw, zꜣt=j and ꜥḥꜥ.
steps: The stative of ꜥḥꜥ for a feminine subject: ꜥḥꜥ.tj.

blocks.html: The last row of the table points ahead: a stative can also follow the object of a verb and describe it, "I found him lying down". That is a circumstantial use, taken up in Circumstantial Clauses.

blocks.title: A noun subject
steps: jw introduces the statement; nṯr "the god" is the subject.
ḥtp.w is the stative of ḥtp "be content", with .w for "he".

blocks.html: Looking for the subject after the stative. Students used to the sḏm=f read mk wj jj.kj with no subject, or take the next word in the sentence as the subject. With the stative the subject comes first; the stative follows like an adjective. Check: look to the left of the verb, not to the right.
